title: Vitamin K2 – The Missing Link in Osteoporosis?
abstract:
**Three Types of Vitamin K**  
There are three known types of vitamin K: [K1, K2, and K3](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/). Among the three, [vitamin K2, or menaquinone](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/), has been shown to promote bone strength and health. K2 is synthesized by [intestinal flora](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/) and can be found in [fermented foods](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/) like natto (fermented soybeans), dairy products, egg yolks, liver, and meat. The most common type of K2 is menaquinone-4 (MK-4). Currently, there is [no recommended daily intake (RDI) set for K2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7353270/) because vitamin K2 is endogenously produced in the human body from K1 and a precursor called [geranylgeranyl (GG)](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student).
Some research suggests that [dietary intake](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/410550) of vitamin K, in general, may not be sufficient for optimal status and may need to be complemented by K1 or K2 supplementation. However, supplementing with just K1 alone may not be sufficient to support bone health, as the conversion of K1 to K2 can be suboptimal. Thus, K2 and GG may be considered [conditionally essential](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student), and supplementation of these nutrients may be recommended for certain individuals.  
**Roles of Vitamin K2 in Bone Health**  
The most direct way vitamin K promotes bone health is through three [vitamin K-dependent proteins in bone and cartilage](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/410550): osteocalcin, matrix γ-carboxyglutamic acid protein, and protein S. [Osteocalcin](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/410550) is a recognized marker of bone formation. Without vitamin K, an essential cofactor for [enzymatic carboxylation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/410550), osteocalcin lacks structural integrity and cannot bind to hydroxyapatite.
Other [bone-supportive roles](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/) of vitamin K include upregulating the transcription of osteoblastic (bone-building) markers, the formation of osteoclasts, and bone resorption. It may also stimulate [osteoblast genesis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7645307/) in bone marrow cells and help reduce [osteoblast apoptosis](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student). Moreover, vitamin K2 (MK-4) has been shown to help stimulate [collagen synthesis in vitro](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student). This might help explain how K2 supports [healthy arterial elasticity](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student) and is partially responsible for [increased bone strength](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student). The [collagen content of bone](https://evolve.elsevier.com/cs/product/9781455774616?role=student) is believed to influence bone strength, elasticity, and fracture risk.
